title: Averages
subtitle: Quantitative Aptitude – Placement Preparation
description: Learn the essential formulas, shortcuts and placement-level problem types based on averages.
learningObjectives: Understand the meaning of arithmetic average.
Find the sum when the average and number of observations are known.
Find the combined average of two or more groups.
Solve questions involving addition, removal or replacement of values.
Use deviations from the average to reduce calculation time.
Solve age, marks, salary, runs and weight-based average problems.
Understand weighted average and average speed.

sections.heading: 1. Meaning of Average
content: An average is a representative value of a group of observations.
In quantitative aptitude, average usually refers to the arithmetic mean.
The arithmetic mean is found by dividing the sum of all observations by the number of observations.
formulas: Average = Sum of observations / Number of observations
Sum of observations = Average × Number of observations
Number of observations = Sum of observations / Average

examples.question: Find the average of 12, 18, 20, 25 and 30.
The average of 8 numbers is 24. Find their total.
examples.solution: Total = Average × Number = 24 × 8 = 192.

sections.heading: 2. Finding a Missing Observation
content: First find the total of all observations using average × number of observations.
Subtract the sum of the known observations from the total.
formulas: Missing value = Required total − Sum of known values

examples.question: The average of five numbers is 28. Four of the numbers are 20, 24, 30 and 36. Find the fifth number.
examples.solution: Required total = 28 × 5 = 140. Sum of known numbers = 20 + 24 + 30 + 36 = 110. Missing number = 140 − 110 = 30.

sections.heading: 3. Average of Consecutive Numbers
content: For consecutive numbers forming an arithmetic sequence, the average is the middle value.
If there is an even number of terms, the average is the mean of the two middle values.
This shortcut also works for consecutive odd numbers and consecutive even numbers.
formulas: Average of consecutive terms = (First term + Last term) / 2
Average of the first n natural numbers = (n + 1) / 2
Average of the first n odd numbers = n
Average of the first n even numbers = n + 1

examples.question: Find the average of 21, 22, 23, 24 and 25.
examples.solution: The middle value is 23. Therefore, the average is 23.

examples.question: Find the average of the first 20 natural numbers.
Find the average of the first 15 odd numbers.
examples.solution: The average of the first n odd numbers is n. Therefore, the average is 15.

sections.heading: 4. Combined Average
content: The combined average of groups cannot usually be found by simply averaging their individual averages.
Each group's average must be multiplied by the number of observations in that group.
Add the group totals and divide by the total number of observations.
formulas: Combined average = [(n1 × a1) + (n2 × a2)] / (n1 + n2)

examples.question: The average marks of 20 students is 60 and the average marks of another 30 students is 70. Find the combined average.
examples.solution: Combined total = (20 × 60) + (30 × 70) = 1200 + 2100 = 3300. Total students = 50. Combined average = 3300 / 50 = 66.

sections.heading: 5. Addition of a New Observation
content: Find the original total using the old average.
Add the new value.
Divide by the new number of observations.
formulas: New average = (Old total + New value) / New count

examples.question: The average age of 5 students is 20 years. A sixth student aged 26 joins them. Find the new average.
examples.solution: Old total = 5 × 20 = 100. New total = 100 + 26 = 126. New average = 126 / 6 = 21 years.

sections.heading: 6. Removal of an Observation
content: Find the original total.
Subtract the removed value.
Divide by the remaining number of observations.
formulas: New average = (Old total − Removed value) / New count

examples.question: The average weight of 8 students is 52 kg. A student weighing 59 kg leaves. Find the average weight of the remaining students.
examples.solution: Old total = 8 × 52 = 416 kg. Remaining total = 416 − 59 = 357 kg. New average = 357 / 7 = 51 kg.

sections.heading: 7. Replacement of an Observation
content: When one value is replaced, only the difference between the old and new values affects the total.
This shortcut avoids recalculating the complete total.
formulas: Change in total = New value − Old value
Change in average = Change in total / Number of observations
New average = Old average + Change in average

examples.question: The average of 10 numbers is 40. One number, 32, is replaced by 52. Find the new average.
examples.solution: Increase in total = 52 − 32 = 20. Increase in average = 20 / 10 = 2. New average = 40 + 2 = 42.

examples.question: The average marks of 20 students was calculated as 65. Later, a mark of 82 was found to have been entered as 62. Find the correct average.
examples.solution: Increase in total = 82 − 62 = 20. Increase in average = 20 / 20 = 1. Correct average = 65 + 1 = 66.

sections.heading: 8. Change in Average
content: A change in average corresponds to a change in the total.
Multiply the change in average by the number of observations to find the change in total.
formulas: Change in total = Number of observations × Change in average

examples.question: The average salary of 12 employees increases by 500. Find the increase in the total salary.
examples.solution: Increase in total = 12 × 500 = 6,000.

examples.question: The average marks of a class of 25 students increases by 0.4 when a wrongly entered mark is corrected. Find the increase in the corrected mark.
examples.solution: Increase in total = 25 × 0.4 = 10. Therefore, the corrected mark is 10 more than the wrongly entered mark.

sections.heading: 9. Deviation Method
content: Choose a convenient assumed average close to the observations.
Find each value's deviation from the assumed average.
Add the deviations and divide by the number of observations.
Add this result to the assumed average.
The sum of deviations from the actual average is always zero.
formulas: Actual average = Assumed average + (Sum of deviations / Number of observations)

examples.question: Find the average of 48, 52, 49, 55 and 46 using 50 as the assumed average.
examples.solution: Deviations from 50 are −2, +2, −1, +5 and −4. Their sum is 0. Average = 50 + 0/5 = 50.

sections.heading: 10. Average Age Problems
content: Age problems commonly involve people joining or leaving a group.
Convert the given average age into total age before making any change.
If every member's age increases by the same number of years, the average also increases by the same number.

examples.question: The average age of 6 employees is 28 years. A manager aged 42 joins them. Find the new average age.
examples.solution: Old total = 6 × 28 = 168. New total = 168 + 42 = 210. New average = 210 / 7 = 30 years.

examples.question: The average age of a group is 24 years. What will be the average age of the same group after 3 years?
examples.solution: Every person's age increases by 3 years. Therefore, the new average is 24 + 3 = 27 years.

sections.heading: 11. Batting Average and Runs
content: Batting-average questions use the same basic relation: total runs divided by number of innings.
To find the runs required to reach a target average, calculate the target total and subtract the present total.
formulas: Batting average = Total runs / Number of innings
Required score = Target total − Present total

examples.question: A player has an average of 45 runs after 8 innings. How many runs must the player score in the ninth innings to raise the average to 48?
examples.solution: Present total = 45 × 8 = 360. Required total after 9 innings = 48 × 9 = 432. Required score = 432 − 360 = 72 runs.

sections.heading: 12. Weighted Average
content: A weighted average is used when different observations or groups do not have equal importance or frequency.
Multiply each value by its weight, add the products and divide by the sum of the weights.
Combined average is a common form of weighted average.
formulas: Weighted average = Sum of (Value × Weight) / Sum of weights

examples.question: A student's test score is 80 with weight 40% and project score is 90 with weight 60%. Find the weighted average.

sections.heading: 13. Average Speed
content: Average speed is total distance divided by total time.
For equal distances travelled at two different speeds, do not take the simple arithmetic mean.
The equal-distance shortcut is the harmonic mean of the two speeds.
formulas: Average speed = Total distance / Total time
For equal distances at speeds x and y: Average speed = 2xy / (x + y)

examples.question: A person travels equal distances at 40 km/h and 60 km/h. Find the average speed.
A car travels for 2 hours at 50 km/h and 3 hours at 70 km/h. Find the average speed.
examples.solution: Total distance = (2 × 50) + (3 × 70) = 100 + 210 = 310 km. Total time = 5 hours. Average speed = 310 / 5 = 62 km/h.

quickShortcuts.title: Convert average to total
quickShortcuts.note: Always use Total = Average × Number before adding, removing or replacing a value.

quickShortcuts.title: Consecutive values
quickShortcuts.note: For equally spaced values, the average is the middle value or the mean of the first and last values.

quickShortcuts.title: Replacement shortcut
quickShortcuts.note: New average = Old average + (New value − Old value) / Number of observations.

quickShortcuts.title: Change in average
quickShortcuts.note: A change of d in the average of n observations changes the total by n × d.

quickShortcuts.title: Same increase for everyone
quickShortcuts.note: If every observation increases by x, the average also increases by x.

quickShortcuts.title: Same multiplication
quickShortcuts.note: If every observation is multiplied by x, the average is also multiplied by x.

quickShortcuts.title: Combined groups
quickShortcuts.note: Use group totals. Do not average two group averages unless the group sizes are equal.

quickShortcuts.title: Equal-distance speed
quickShortcuts.note: For two equal distances, use 2xy / (x + y), not (x + y) / 2.

placementQuestionTypes: Addition or removal of a person
commonMistakes: Adding group averages without considering the group sizes.
Forgetting to convert an average into a total before adding or removing an observation.
Dividing by the old count after a new observation joins.
Dividing by the original count after an observation leaves.
Using the simple arithmetic mean for equal-distance average-speed questions.
Recalculating every value when the replacement shortcut can be used.
Confusing a change in total with a change in average.
Using the middle-value shortcut for numbers that are not equally spaced.

I can solve age and batting-average problems.
